signatures.label: Brake pad wear indicator contacting the rotor
signatures.hint: Classically loudest when NOT braking and quiets when the pedal is pressed — the tab is pushed away from the disc.
signatures.why: The wear tab is a deliberate warning: friction material is near its limit but the pad is still working.
confirm: Look through the wheel spokes at pad thickness — under ~3 mm needs replacement
Check whether the noise stops when the brake pedal is applied
Inspect both sides of each axle; wear is often uneven
discriminators: Does the noise go away when you press the brake pedal?
Is it there at low speed with the windows down, without braking?

signatures.label: Brake pads worn through to the backing plate
signatures.hint: Grinding that appears only under braking, often with a vibration through the pedal.
signatures.why: Friction material is gone. Stopping distance is compromised and the rotor is being destroyed.
confirm: Do not road-test further than necessary
Inspect pads — backing plate visible against the rotor confirms it
Check rotor surface for deep scoring; it will likely need replacing, not machining
discriminators: Does it happen only while braking?
Do you feel it through the pedal?

signatures.label: Sticking caliper or seized slide pin
signatures.hint: Usually one corner only, often with a hot wheel and a burning smell after driving.
signatures.why: A dragging caliper overheats the rotor and pad, pulls the car under braking and destroys fuel economy.
confirm: After a short drive, compare wheel temperature side to side — carefully
Jack the corner and check the wheel spins freely
Inspect slide pins for dry or corroded travel
discriminators: Is it just one corner?
Does the car pull to one side when braking?
Is one wheel noticeably hotter after a drive?

signatures.label: Rotor thickness variation (commonly called warped rotors)
signatures.hint: Pulsing you feel in the pedal or steering wheel, worst braking from high speed.
signatures.why: Uneven pad deposits or disc thickness variation make braking torque fluctuate once per revolution.
confirm: Measure disc thickness variation with a micrometer at eight points
Check lateral runout with a dial gauge
Inspect for uneven pad transfer film
discriminators: Do you feel a pulse in the pedal?
Is it worse braking from motorway speed?

signatures.label: Bent dust shield touching the rotor
signatures.hint: Light scraping in step with wheel speed that is unaffected by braking. Cheapest thing on this list.
signatures.why: The thin backing plate has been knocked into the disc — usually by a kerb or during a tyre change.
confirm: Spin the wheel off the ground and listen
Look for a bright rub mark on the shield
Bend the shield clear with a screwdriver and re-test
discriminators: Does braking change the noise at all?
Has the car been on a kerb or had wheels off recently?

signatures.label: Worn wheel bearing
signatures.hint: Rises with road speed, not engine RPM, and changes as you sway the car left and right.
signatures.why: The bearing races are pitted. Left long enough a bearing can seize or allow the hub to move.
confirm: Sway test: gentle S-turns at 60-80 km/h — loading the bad side usually makes it louder
Jack the wheel, rock it at 12 and 6 o'clock for play
Spin by hand and listen at the hub
discriminators: Does it change when you swerve gently left and right?
Does it track road speed rather than engine speed?
Is it still there in neutral coasting?

signatures.label: Cupped or feathered tyre wear
signatures.hint: Very close to a bearing noise, but usually unchanged by swerving and often changes after a tyre rotation.
signatures.why: Irregular tread wear from worn dampers, misalignment or under-inflation makes the tread pattern noisy.
confirm: Run a hand across the tread — cupping feels like scallops
Rotate the tyres and see whether the noise moves
Check alignment and damper condition
discriminators: Does gentle swerving change it?
Did the noise change after the last tyre rotation?

signatures.label: Broken tyre belt or flat-spotted tyre
signatures.hint: One thump per wheel revolution, often with a visible bulge or a vibration that peaks at a specific speed.
signatures.why: A separated belt can fail suddenly at speed.
confirm: Inspect each tyre for bulges or flat spots
Spin each wheel off the ground and watch for wobble
Have the tyres road-force balanced
discriminators: Is it exactly one thump per wheel turn?
Is there a bulge visible on any sidewall or tread?

signatures.label: Worn outer CV joint
signatures.hint: Rhythmic clicking on full lock, worse under power. Reversing in a tight circle usually amplifies it.
signatures.why: The joint has lost grease or taken in water through a split boot, and the bearing cage is worn.
confirm: Drive slow tight circles both directions in an empty car park
Inspect CV boots for splits and thrown grease
Check for play by twisting the shaft at the joint
discriminators: Is it worse on full lock?
Does it change between left and right turns?
Is there grease flung around inside the wheel arch?

signatures.label: Worn inner CV / tripod joint
signatures.hint: A shudder or clunk on hard acceleration from a stop, felt through the floor rather than heard.
signatures.why: The tripod bearing has worn a groove in its housing, so it binds under torque.
confirm: Accelerate hard from rest in a straight line and feel for shudder
Inspect the inner boot
Check for play by pushing and pulling the shaft axially
discriminators: Does it happen mostly on hard acceleration from a stop?
Is it a shudder rather than a click?

signatures.label: Worn universal joint in the propshaft
signatures.hint: A clunk when taking up drive, sometimes a dry squeak at low speed that tracks road speed.
signatures.why: A failed U-joint can drop the propshaft, which is dangerous at speed.
confirm: Grip the propshaft and try to rotate it against the flange — any play is too much
Look for rust-coloured dust around the bearing caps
Check for a dry squeak that rises with speed
discriminators: Is there a clunk when moving off or changing between drive and reverse?
Is the vehicle rear- or four-wheel drive?

signatures.label: Worn differential ring and pinion
signatures.hint: A howl that changes character between coasting and pulling at the same speed.
signatures.why: Gear-set wear or incorrect backlash. Often traceable to low or degraded gear oil.
confirm: Note whether it howls on drive, on coast, or both — this points at the wear pattern
Check diff oil level and condition for metal
Listen with the vehicle on a lift under load
discriminators: Does the noise differ between accelerating and coasting at the same speed?
Has the diff oil ever been changed?

signatures.label: Worn anti-roll bar link or bush
signatures.hint: The most common cause of a rattle over small bumps at low speed. Often worse on rough surfaces than big potholes.
signatures.why: The ball joint in the link has worn loose, so it knocks as the bar twists.
confirm: With the car on the ground, push down hard on each corner and listen
Grip each link and try to move it — any play is a fail
Pry-bar test the bushes on a lift
discriminators: Is it worse over small, sharp bumps rather than big ones?
Does it happen when only one wheel hits a bump?

signatures.label: Worn strut top mount or bearing
signatures.hint: A clunk or groan you can reproduce standing still, just by turning the wheel lock to lock.
signatures.why: The bearing that lets the strut rotate with the steering has failed, or the rubber mount has separated.
confirm: Turn the wheel lock to lock while stationary with the window down
Have someone bounce the corner while you feel the top mount
Inspect for separated or cracked rubber
discriminators: Can you reproduce it standing still by turning the wheel?
Does the steering feel notchy as it returns to centre?

signatures.label: Worn lower ball joint
signatures.hint: Similar to a sway bar link, but tends to clunk under braking and over larger inputs too.
signatures.why: A ball joint that separates drops the wheel out of the arch. This one is worth being conservative about.
confirm: Support the control arm, pry between the arm and knuckle for vertical play
Check the boot for splits and grease loss
Compare tyre wear on the inner and outer edges
discriminators: Does it also clunk when braking?
Is the steering vague or wandering?

signatures.label: Perished control arm bush
signatures.hint: Often a dull clunk on braking or a groan as the car rocks fore and aft.
signatures.why: The rubber has torn or the fluid-filled bush has emptied, so the arm moves before it loads.
confirm: Pry-bar the bush and look for movement or torn rubber
Look for a bush that has visibly shifted off centre
Check alignment — worn bushes usually throw camber and caster out
discriminators: Is it worst on braking?
Does the steering pull under braking?

signatures.label: Failing power steering pump or low fluid
signatures.hint: Rises as you turn the wheel and peaks at full lock. Worst when cold.
signatures.why: Aerated or low fluid, or a worn pump, makes the vanes cavitate under load.
confirm: Check fluid level and look for foam or dark colour
Listen at the pump while someone turns the wheel
Inspect the low-pressure hose for a leak drawing in air
discriminators: Does it peak at full lock?
Is it loudest when the engine is cold?
Is the steering heavier than it used to be?

signatures.label: Worn tie rod end
signatures.hint: A knock felt through the steering wheel over rough surfaces, with vague on-centre feel.
signatures.why: Steering play. A separated tie rod means total loss of steering on that wheel.
confirm: Rock the wheel at 3 and 9 o'clock with the car raised
Have someone rock the steering wheel while you watch the joint
Check the boot for splits
discriminators: Do you feel the knock in the steering wheel itself?
Does the car wander on the motorway?

signatures.label: Broken coil spring
signatures.hint: A hard clunk plus one corner sitting lower than the other side.
signatures.why: A broken coil can contact the tyre and cut it.
confirm: Measure ride height at each corner and compare side to side
Inspect the spring visually, especially the bottom two coils
Look for a bright witness mark where the spring end has moved
discriminators: Does one corner sit lower?
Was there a sharp bang before the noise started?

signatures.label: Worn shock absorber or strut
signatures.hint: The car keeps bouncing after a bump, and the noise comes with a floaty ride.
signatures.why: Loss of damping fluid means the spring is no longer controlled.
confirm: Bounce test each corner — it should settle in one rebound
Look for oil film down the damper body
Check for cupped tyre wear as corroborating evidence
discriminators: Does the car float or wallow over undulations?
Is there oil on the damper body?

signatures.label: Valvetrain clearance / lifter tick
signatures.hint: Ticks at half engine speed and is often loudest cold, quieting as oil pressure builds.
signatures.why: Excess clearance, a collapsed hydraulic lifter, or oil that is too thin or too dirty to fill the lifter.
confirm: Note whether it fades as the engine warms — a fading tick points at lifters
Check oil level and service history
Use a stethoscope on the valve cover to localise the cylinder
discriminators: Does it fade once warm?
Is the tick at half engine speed rather than engine speed?
When was the last oil change?

signatures.label: Connecting rod bearing knock
signatures.hint: A deep knock that gets worse under load and often quietens briefly if you disable that cylinder's injector or plug.
signatures.why: Bearing clearance has opened up. Continued running will destroy the crankshaft.
confirm: Stop driving the vehicle
Check oil for metallic glitter
Cylinder cut-out test: the knock usually softens when the offending cylinder is disabled
Check oil pressure with a mechanical gauge
discriminators: Does it get louder under load rather than just with RPM?
Is there any metallic glitter in the oil?
Has oil pressure dropped?

signatures.label: Detonation / pre-ignition (pinking)
signatures.hint: Sounds like marbles in a can, only under load — climbing a hill or accelerating in too high a gear.
signatures.why: The fuel-air charge is igniting uncontrolled. Sustained detonation holes pistons.
confirm: Try a tank of higher-octane fuel and see whether it disappears
Scan for knock sensor and timing correction data
Check for carbon build-up and cooling system function
discriminators: Only under load, never at idle?
Worse on hot days or up hills?
What octane fuel is being used versus what the manufacturer specifies?

signatures.label: Exhaust manifold leak or cracked manifold
signatures.hint: A ticking that is loudest on a cold start and quietens as the metal expands and seals.
signatures.why: A broken stud or cracked manifold lets pulses escape. It can also draw in air and skew fuel trims.
confirm: Listen on a cold start — it should quieten as the engine warms
Feel carefully for escaping pulses near the manifold flange
Look for black soot tracks around the gasket
discriminators: Is it loudest in the first minute after a cold start?
Does it fade rather than get worse as the engine warms?

signatures.label: Stretched timing chain or failing tensioner
signatures.hint: A brief rattle in the first seconds after a cold start, from the front or rear of the engine.
signatures.why: A chain that jumps a tooth can destroy an interference engine in one revolution.
confirm: Scan for camshaft/crankshaft correlation codes
Compare cam timing against spec with a scope or by inspection
Check oil condition — chain wear is usually an oil-maintenance story
discriminators: Is the rattle only for a second or two on a cold start?
Any check engine light for cam/crank correlation?

signatures.label: Glazed, loose or misaligned serpentine belt
signatures.hint: Loudest on a cold, damp start, and when a load is applied — air conditioning on, or steering at full lock.
signatures.why: The belt is slipping. Either its tension is gone or the ribs are glazed.
confirm: Spray a little water on the belt: if the noise changes momentarily, it is belt-related
Inspect ribs for glazing, cracking and missing chunks
Check tensioner travel and pulley alignment
discriminators: Is it worse when cold or damp?
Does switching the air conditioning on change it?

signatures.label: Failing idler or tensioner pulley bearing
signatures.hint: Tracks engine RPM and stays when the belt is removed only if the noise is from a driven accessory — not the pulley itself.
signatures.why: A dry bearing. If it seizes it will shred the belt and take out the water pump drive with it.
confirm: Remove the belt and spin each pulley by hand, feeling for roughness
Use a stethoscope on each pulley centre with the engine running
Briefly run the engine without the belt to see if the noise disappears
discriminators: Does the noise track engine speed exactly?
Does it persist in neutral with the engine revved?

signatures.label: Worn alternator bearing
signatures.hint: A whine that changes when electrical load changes — headlights and rear demister on.
signatures.why: Bearing wear, or a failing rectifier making an electrical whine.
confirm: Switch on headlights and demister — an electrical whine changes pitch
Stethoscope the alternator case
Test charging output and AC ripple
discriminators: Does turning on high electrical loads change the noise?
Any flickering lights or battery warning?

signatures.label: Failing water pump bearing or seal
signatures.hint: RPM-linked growl plus a coolant weep from the pump's telltale hole.
signatures.why: A seized pump means immediate overheating, and on belt-driven engines it can strip the timing belt.
confirm: Look for crusty coolant residue at the weep hole
Check for play by rocking the pulley
Check coolant level and for any sweet smell
discriminators: Is there any coolant residue near the pump?
Has the temperature gauge been higher than normal?

signatures.label: Vacuum leak
signatures.hint: A steady hiss at idle, usually with an unsteady or high idle and lean fuel trims.
signatures.why: Unmetered air is entering after the mass airflow sensor, so the mixture goes lean.
confirm: Check long-term fuel trims — lean at idle, normalising at higher RPM, points to a leak
Smoke-test the intake
Inspect intake boots and PCV hoses for splits
discriminators: Is the idle unsteady?
Any lean codes stored?

signatures.label: Worn clutch release (throwout) bearing
signatures.hint: Appears the moment you press the clutch and vanishes when you let it out.
signatures.why: The bearing that pushes the pressure plate is worn. Replaced with the clutch, since the gearbox has to come out anyway.
confirm: At idle in neutral, press the clutch and listen for the noise appearing
Compare against the input shaft bearing test (noise with clutch out)
Check clutch pedal free play
discriminators: Does it appear when you press the clutch, or when you release it?
Is it there in neutral with the clutch up?

signatures.label: Worn gearbox input shaft bearing
signatures.hint: The mirror image of the release bearing: present in neutral with the clutch UP, disappears when you press the clutch.
signatures.why: The bearing supporting the input shaft is worn.
confirm: In neutral at idle, listen with the clutch up, then press it — if the noise goes, it is the input shaft
Check gearbox oil level and condition
Listen for the noise changing in different gears
discriminators: Does pressing the clutch make it quieter or louder?

signatures.label: Torque converter lock-up shudder
signatures.hint: Feels like driving over rumble strips for a couple of seconds at a steady light-throttle cruise, often 60-80 km/h.
signatures.why: The lock-up clutch is slipping as it engages, usually from degraded fluid.
confirm: Note the exact speed and throttle position where it happens
Check transmission fluid level, colour and smell
Watch lock-up clutch slip rate on a scan tool
discriminators: Does it happen at a steady light-throttle cruise around a specific speed?
Does it stop instantly if you touch the brake or accelerate harder?

signatures.label: Automatic transmission pump whine / low fluid
signatures.hint: A whine that changes with gear selection — check it in Park, Neutral, Drive and Reverse.
signatures.why: Usually low or aerated fluid. Running a transmission low destroys it quickly.
confirm: Check fluid level using the manufacturer's exact procedure and temperature
Inspect fluid for a burnt smell or dark colour
Note whether the whine differs between Park, Reverse and Drive
discriminators: Does the whine change when you select a gear?
When was the fluid last changed?

signatures.label: Worn synchroniser
signatures.hint: Grinding into one specific gear — most often second — while the others are clean.
signatures.why: The synchro cone can no longer match shaft speeds in the time you give it.
confirm: Establish which gear or gears grind, and whether it happens cold only
Try double-clutching — if that cures it, the synchro is the suspect
Check gearbox oil level and specification
discriminators: Which gear grinds?
Is it worse when the gearbox is cold?
Does slowing the shift down avoid it?

signatures.label: Loose exhaust heat shield
signatures.hint: A tinny buzz that shows up in a narrow RPM band and disappears above and below it.
signatures.why: A corroded mounting tab lets the thin shield resonate.
confirm: Tap along the shields with the engine off — the loose one buzzes
Hold the shield with a gloved hand while someone holds the RPM
Fit a large washer and clamp, or a hose clamp, as a permanent fix
discriminators: Does it happen only in a narrow RPM range?
Does it stop if you touch the shield?

signatures.label: Blowing exhaust joint or corroded section
signatures.hint: Volume rises with throttle, and there is often a resonant drone at one cruising speed.
signatures.why: Beyond noise, a leak ahead of the cabin can put exhaust gas inside the car.
confirm: With the engine cold, block the tailpipe briefly and listen for escaping gas
Inspect joints and welds for black soot streaks
Check for any exhaust smell inside the cabin — treat that as urgent
discriminators: Can you smell exhaust inside the car?
Is it louder under acceleration?

signatures.label: Air conditioning compressor or clutch failure
signatures.hint: Only present with the air conditioning switched on, and stops the moment you switch it off.
signatures.why: The clutch bearing or the compressor itself is failing. A seizure will shred the belt.
confirm: Toggle the air conditioning on and off and confirm the noise follows it
Watch the clutch engage and disengage
Check refrigerant charge and compressor oil
discriminators: Does switching the air conditioning off silence it completely?

signatures.label: Blower motor bearing wear or debris in the fan
signatures.hint: Changes with fan speed setting and is unaffected by engine RPM or road speed.
signatures.why: Leaves or a dry bearing in the heater box.
confirm: Cycle the fan through every speed with the engine off
Remove the cabin filter and check for debris
Inspect the blower wheel
discriminators: Does the noise change with the fan speed dial?
Is it there with the engine off?

signatures.label: Failing fuel pump
signatures.hint: A whine from the fuel tank area that gets worse as the tank empties, sometimes with hesitation under load.
signatures.why: The pump is straining, often because it is worn or the filter is blocked. Failure leaves you stranded.
confirm: Note whether the noise worsens below a quarter tank
Test fuel pressure under load, not just at idle
Check the fuel filter service interval
discriminators: Is it worse with a low tank?
Any hesitation or stumble under hard acceleration?

signatures.label: Collapsed engine or gearbox mount
signatures.hint: A clunk when taking up drive or lifting off, with more vibration through the cabin at idle.
signatures.why: The rubber has torn or the fluid-filled mount has emptied, so the powertrain moves under torque.
confirm: With the handbrake on, gently load the drivetrain in drive and reverse and watch engine movement
Inspect mounts for torn rubber or leaked fluid
Check for contact marks where the engine has moved into something
discriminators: Is the clunk when you take up drive or change direction?
Has idle vibration in the cabin got worse?

signatures.label: Broken catalytic converter substrate
signatures.hint: Sounds like gravel in a tin. Reproduce it by tapping the converter with a rubber mallet when cold.
signatures.why: The ceramic honeycomb has broken up. Fragments can block the exhaust and cause serious power loss.
confirm: Tap the converter with a rubber mallet when cold and listen for loose material
Check for power loss and exhaust back-pressure
Scan for catalyst efficiency codes
discriminators: Does it rattle when you tap the exhaust with the engine off?
Has the car lost power, especially at higher speeds?
